scenes.text: Want someone to like you more? Ask them for a small favor.
This is called the Ben Franklin effect.
When Franklin served in the Pennsylvania Assembly, a fellow lawmaker opposed him.
Instead of flattering him, Franklin asked to borrow a rare book from his library.
The rival lent it, and Franklin returned it about a week later with a thank you note.
The next time they met, the man spoke to him kindly for the first time.
They stayed friends until the man died.
Franklin later told this story in his autobiography.
In nineteen sixty nine, psychologists Jecker and Landy tested the idea.
Students won money in a quiz.
Afterwards, the researcher personally asked some of them to give the money back as a favor.
Those students liked him the most.
When a secretary asked instead, liking was lowest.
Psychologists think our minds want our actions and feelings to match.
Other researchers think a favor request feels like a friendly invitation.
Would you try this on someone who doesn't like you?

title: Ask for a favor and they'll like you more? 🤝
caption: Ben Franklin won over a rival by borrowing a rare book. A 1969 study by Jecker and Landy found a similar effect. 📚
